cursor.note: THIS END OWNS THE CAPTURE AND THE RECIPE DOOR. device.py's _CLOSURE_RUNNER wraps the proof and reports its closure at exit; _read_closure DISCARDS a closure that cannot name its own proof, so seal-taking and re-checking apply the same predicate — the measured defect (2026-09-08) that made a just-sealed green proof read expired, because a proof outside the repo produced an EMPTY closure whose sha256 was e3b0c442. A tree_moved guard falls back to the pre-run directory hash when the tree shifted under the run. validation_store.sealed_fingerprint_now is the ONE DOOR that picks the recipe by what the seal carries, so a pre-closure seal is still re-checked the way it was TAKEN, and standing()'s sentence names the scope three ways (artifact / N imported files / the directory). || a seal now fingerprints WHAT THE PROOF IMPORTS, not the directory it sits in. run_proof runs the proof under an atexit+runpy wrapper that reports sys.modules' repo-relative __file__ set; the seal records evidence.fingerprint_closure and a hash over exactly that set. MEASURED: on cairn/tools/base's 36 sealed proofs a touch to transitions.py expired 36 of 36 under the old recipe and expires 15 of 36 now — 21 seals survive, 0 capture failures. Capture cost on an idle machine -0.029s/run (-1.7%), below run-to-run variance, against >=35.7s of re-seals saved per edit. Corpus census 82 standing (41.4%) -> 120 standing (60.6%). Verdict artifact verdict-20260908T153550-70df7db84b66.json: both criteria pass, all four hypotheses confirmed. WHAT A READER SHOULD KNOW IN A YEAR: the two proofs that separated (test_nest.py, test_transitions.py) sit in the SAME directory, which is why the directory recipe could never have told them apart.
